utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have appearances now, this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I am Eric Ostberg. I appear today with Mr. Giuliano Turone, Ms. Teresa McHenry and Ms. Elles van Dusschoten. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now appearances on the defence? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honour. My name is Edina Residovic. I am the defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, appearing together with my co-counsel, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Zjelko Olujic. I am the defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. Together with me in the courtroom is Mr. Michael Greaves, an attorney from the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. Tom Moran for Hazim Delic. My lead counsel, as the court knows, is out of the city on business.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. John Ackerman, appearing on behalf of Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Sorry, your co-counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is Cynthia McMurrey. She is out of town and will be back in town next Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. Howard Morrison appearing on my own on the issue of contempt only regarding the allegation of such against Mr. Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are delighted to have all of you here. Now we want to state the position of the Trial Chamber, because we had the position of both the counsel for the prosecution and defence in this matter and we have not stated the position of the Trial Chamber, and this we intend to do now. The incident which brought about this whole episode is very fresh and it has kept on repeating and has stalled the principal proceedings in this Trial Chamber. Now on 15th May the Prosecutor made a complaint that his attention had been drawn to a publication in Slobodan Herzegovina, the Sarajevo weekly, containing an interview with Delalic, one of the accused persons on trial before us. The publication had been inset, a list of the prosecution witnesses, including those protected on the Order of this Trial Chamber. There was a comment two weeks later in the same publications. The two publications were turned out to this Trial Chamber. Counsel defending the accused persons were visibly concerned by the complaint. They protested and withdrew participation in the proceedings until the suspicion of their complicity in the circumstances surrounding the publication was investigated and cleared. The Prosecutor's oral assurances to defence counsel that no suspicions fell on them did not satisfy them. The prosecution has now gone forward in writing to clarify the position. On 16th May the Trial Chamber referred the complaint to the President to investigate the allegation and report to the Trial Chamber. The following Terms of Reference, and I read them: "1: To investigate the circumstances of the leakage of the information. 2: To make a determination as to responsibility or otherwise of any (i) counsel appearing in the Celebici proceedings and (ii) other persons connected with the custody of the witness lists. 3: To determine the effect of the leakage upon the current proceedings. 4: To report back to the Trial Chamber". On 28th May the President reported to the Trial Chamber. You all have copies of his reports. The report cleared Ms Residovic and Professor O'Sullivan, counsel to the first accused, Delalic, of misconduct, as there was no evidence against them. The Trial Chamber accepts this recommendation. With respect to Delalic, the report stated that on interview by the President he denied holding a telephone interview with anybody and claimed his right to silence. The President got in touch with Tahir Pervan, the alleged interviewer of Delalic in the publication, on the telephone, who claimed his right to silence and refused to speak. Mr. Pervan at first offered to come to The Hague to give evidence, since he was afraid to give any evidence in Sarajevo, but subsequently claimed he had lost his passport and could not travel. The subsequent effort to speak to Pervan was answered by his counsel, who told the President he had advised his client not to answer any questions. The President did not speak to the editor of the paper. The report does not disclose he had spoken to any other person. However, in his conclusion the President found that Delalic might have held the interview credited to him and in the course of interview might have named at least one of the witnesses in the list of witnesses published. He accordingly suggested that Delalic might be charged with the contempt of the Tribunal. The Trial Chamber finds it difficult to accept this recommendation. The only evidence before the learned President was the unequivocal and uncontradicted denial of Delalic of the accusation founded on the publication. There is no evidence on which the President could have relied on casting any doubts on the denial. Accordingly the supposition by the President that Delalic might have given the interview has no necessary evidence and cannot constitute a rational basis for a judicial finding against Delalic. The Trial Chamber, therefore, is unable to accept that finding. The position of the Trial Chamber is that Delalic still stands on his accusation. It is nowhere justified by the reference which the President made to suggest his being charged for contempt. That is our position. We have heard you. I think this is the last the Trial Chamber will have about this matter. It has spent so much time dealing with it and it has held up an important aspect of a matter, which is perhaps more serious than the furor which the delay has caused. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I appear on behalf of Mr. Delalic concerning this particular matter alone. May I say that, of course, he will be no doubt pleased to hear the conclusion of the Trial Chamber that the Trial Chamber has concluded that there is no evidence and therefore no basis for continuing the suspicion in the mind of the Trial Chamber that he was guilty of the contempt alleged or indeed any contempt. May I make it perfectly plain that Mr. Delalic's position is this and has always been, that he did not seek the delay of this matter. He wants the trial to continue and he wants it to continue upon the basis of the understanding that he was in no way responsible for the publication of either the articles or the names of any witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think our position is very clear. I do not think we need say anything. We do not want to continue the incrimination and carrying on with this matter. I think we have had enough of it. Let us carry on with the principal proceedings for which we are here. If the prosecution has any witnesses to call today, we will decide to take them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, due to the incident and the delay and the stay, we had to from economical and other reasons in cooperation with the Victim and Witness Unit to send witnesses back. We have had them on hold and we have not, being unaware of what was going to be the decision of the court, yet brought them back to The Hague. We are prepared to do so. If we are lucky, we can have some of them here tomorrow. If we are not lucky, we cannot have them here until Monday. That is the position. Today we cannot have them, because the witnesses and victims unit considered it in consultation with the prosecution considered it impossible from economical and other reasons to have them sitting waiting in The Hague. So that is the position of us. Maybe tomorrow; certainly on Monday. Thank you, your Honour. I can find that out during the day. I can give you the view of the Victim Witness Unit on the exact moment when we can have our first witness back in The Hague. That I can do today. By the way, I want to express the feelings of the prosecution and utter my satisfaction over the position taken by the Trial Chamber on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Outside that, I think that we have a few motions which have been outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we might be able to take that, any of them, if counsel is disposed to, because we have a list of them. The first one is the joint motion by defendants on the production of evidence by the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if I might mention this, please? I wonder whether we might have 20 minutes just to prepare. We were not quite expecting your Honour to continue quite so quickly. I am hesitant to get up and ask for yet further delay, but perhaps we can just draw breath for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can then rise and come back at 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please do inform the defence of the witnesses you want to examine next, because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do inform the defence of the witness you wish to examine, because they complain "we have not prepared that witness for cross-examination".

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I will do that after the break, your Honour. I will have to consult with the witness unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before you have leave, while the prosecution is still here, it would be helpful to know who the witnesses they think they are going to get here and when, so we could be prepared to cross-examine them and not stand here and complain we did not know those particular witnesses were coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is exactly what I have told Mr. Ostberg.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am sorry. I was sitting over here sleeping, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought it was in relation to which of the witnesses is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: You will have the answer 40 minutes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Before we rise, if you can just read out the list of motions we are talking about, I know I have at least one outstanding that I am probably going to withdraw -- in fact I am going to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I have read the first one, the joint motion by the defence on the production of evidence by the prosecution. Second one is the defendant Hazim Delic's designation of an expert witness. The third is Delic's motion to strike out Prosecution Exhibits 1 and 2. The fourth, Prosecution's motion to compel the disclosure of the addresses of witnesses. The fifth, Prosecution motion for leave to call Mr. Regis Abribat as a witness, although we have not had any response to that. The sixth, Prosecution motion to specify the documents disclosed by the Prosecutor that Delalic's defence intended to use as evidence. Also there has been no response, but if counsel is ready, we might as well take them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the motion to strike Prosecution 1 and 2 that I filed, that is the one that I am going to withdraw. I was going to file later today. To save everybody the time finding it I checked the record. It is my error. It turns out the issue has been presented. There is no reason to do it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Also in case it would assist, in respect of the motion of Mr. Delic for designation of an expert witness, the prosecution has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: So it is not necessary to argue. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, as for the motion filed by the Prosecutor regarding the evidence to be used by the defence of Mr. Delalic, we are prepared to present our response today in the course of the hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now before the Trial Chamber rises, I wish to express the appreciation of the Trial Chamber and everyone concerned to Mr. Morrison for his very capable way of presenting the case of his client in an empassioned and an emotional matter, which matter which concerns a lot of emotions. We are very pleased that you have presented the arguments fairly, assisted the prosecution and the Trial Chamber and presented a balanced view of what counsel should do in circumstances of this nature, to be completely detached and to be helpful to everybody. That is a very good evidence of the tradition and I am very, very pleased to thank you and to congratulate you for all the efforts. I believe your colleagues also admire the way you have handled the matter. Thank you very much. We appreciate it very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour and your colleagues, thank you for those kind comments. May I offer my thanks for the professional courtesy and friendship which has been shown to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble at 11. (10.25 am) (Short break) (11.05 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will begin with the first motion, the motion on the production of evidence by the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. This motion was filed by the defence seeking supplementary rules of evidence and to this motion the prosecution objects that such a request of supplementary rules is, in the submission of the prosecution, unnecessary and unreasonable, since all is already ruled in our rules of evidence and procedure, and particularly in Rules 66 and following. I will say that the crucial sentences in the motion of the defence are the following, as far as the legal arguments are concerned. In the motion we read that: "The prosecution in the opinion of the defence lawyers has conspicuously failed to serve upon the defence any statement from a number of the witnesses on its witness list." We read again in the motion that: "Such failure means that each defendant can have no idea until that witness gets into the witness box what case he has to meet in respect of that particular witness". Well, your Honours, we believe that all this is simply not true. First of all, with respect to witnesses who appear on the witness list but for whom the defence does not have witness statements, simply the reason is that no witness statement exists for limited number of witnesses. As a matter of fact, the prosecution has complied with its obligations in good faith and completely and will continue to do so. As I say, there is a small number of witnesses for which no previous witness statement exists, but even for these witnesses it is not really true that defendants have no idea of what these witnesses would testify on. If we see our witness list, we might see that one of these witnesses for which no previous statement exists was, for instance, the first one, Mr. Beelen, but in our witness list it is stated quite clearly that this man coming from the Netherlands police should give a physical description of Celebici camp with maps, videos, pictures and model. We provided the defence lawyers in due time with a written report done by Mr. Beelen. Another witness like this for which no technical witness statement existed but we had a report on what the testimony would be was Ms Calic, our expert witness on general background. Dr O is another example, but in our witness list filed on March 7th we explained he is a physician. He visited and issued medical certificates on a number of former detainees of Celebici camp, etc. So I would say that the prosecution could not even be able to respond more specifically to this motion because the defence has not provided any specifics, but only made some vague allegations. So the prosecution can only try to divine, to guess, what the estimated colleagues of the defence are exactly concerned about. So the prosecution might try to define that one instance which the defence might be referring to is maybe the one concerning Mr. Thomas Moerbauer of the Austrian Federal Police, who is referred to in the prosecution witness list at number 23 as being supposed to testify, and I quote from the witness list: "On the arrest of Delalic and Mucic and the seizure of documents pertaining to them and for whom no previous statement exists". But even about Mr. Moerbauer the prosecution with a letter dated 17th December 1996 offered to all defence lawyers a copy of the report, of the big report of the federal police of Vienna. Mr. Moerbauer, his name and signature appear as one of the authors of the report, and all defence lawyers have now a copy of this report. Other instances where the prosecution might believe that it might guess as to what the defence is referring to might concern statements which were provided by another defence counsel to the Prosecution, but as reported in the status hearing of 1st November 1996, the defence apparently generally agreed that the defence would exchange material among itself and was not requesting that the prosecution provide disclosure of material provided by one defence attorney to the prosecution. So we do not know exactly actually what to add more about this motion. We can emphasise that in our rules if there is some complaint about recent disclosures we have Rule 67D, which provides that: "If either party discovers additional evidence or material which should have been produced earlier pursuant to the Rules, that party shall promptly notify the other party and the Trial Chamber of the existence of the additional evidence or material". This is what we have done always in due time and in perfect good faith. So the prosecution believes that no justification exists for adopting additional rules of evidence whatsoever. This, I think, is all I can say about this motion. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we hear you, Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There are two problems, one of which, in my respectful submission, has simply not been addressed by my friend, Mr. Turone, at all in the course of his submissions, and I will deal with that first so I can bring it to your attention. Your Honours perhaps have not yet penetrated beyond the wall here, but you will know we have a defence room, now two defence rooms, where counsel gather. Sometimes during the course of the day a very nice young man who is plainly employed by the Office of the Prosecution will suddenly appear with a large number of pieces of paper in his hand and we have to sign for them. They are a variety of documents. For example, some of these documents which have been shown to witnesses where they have signed confession to possessing arms are provided to us. Sometimes it is a witness statement, often dated quite a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: suddenly emerged from the woodwork and we had to sign for it. This is the sort of document we are given. There is no indication given to us whatsoever, no doubt because the very nice young man is not given any himself to give to us, as to what purpose those documents are being given to us for. There are two possible explanations, in my respectful submission. One, it is being served by the prosecution as additional evidence; in other words, evidence upon which the prosecution relies and which they are serving on us so that we may know what the witness is likely to say. The alternative is that it is being served as exculpatory material, and I use that word within the definition of the rules, a statement of a witness who is to be called by the prosecution but one which is inconsistent in some way with the statement which they have served on us, as it were, as part of the prosecution bundle, and therefore it is available to us to cross-examine the witness on a previous inconsistent statement. The problem is this. At no stage are we told which of those two purposes is being served by the service of that document. It is sometimes really rather difficult to work it out, and it makes preparing cross-examination of a particular witness extraordinarily difficult if you do not know whether the prosecution relies on this document or is simply giving it to you so that you know that this inconsistent statement exists in some way. That is the first concern that we have. Material is coming through our door pretty well daily without explanation as to what purpose it is being given to us for. That, in my respectful submission, is inherently unfair, not to know what the purpose of this document is. The second problem is this, and this is the matter that my learned friend, Mr. Turone, has addressed. There are a number of witnesses set out in the Prosecution witness list in respect of whom no statement of any kind has ever been served upon us. Let me give you an example. There is a gentleman who I suspect is a general in the army of the kingdom of the Netherlands, a man by the name of de Vogel. I think he must be an expert witness. Nothing has been served on us at all to indicate the nature of the evidence he might give. If he is an expert witness, there may come a time when he is called by the prosecution, and we are taken by surprise. We are then going to be put in the position where we are going to be applying to your Honours for an adjournment so that we can instruct an expert, because it is only at that point that we find out what this man is going to say and it may take us a very considerable amount of time to go and instruct a similar expert. In my respectful submission to be forced into that situation is outrageous actually. No other word for it. What is going to happen is that this court is going to find itself presented by the failure of the prosecution to do its job properly with a situation where yet another serious delay is going to be caused by their not serving any indication what these people are going to save. I pick that one out as a particular example, because this falls perhaps into two categories. First of all, it concerns the rules about expert witnesses and secondly it concerns the general proposition I have just laid before you, but there are other people. It is one thing, and I note that the report by Mr. Moerbauer is referred to. It is one thing for somebody to have a report. It is quite another to have a statement from someone which contains at the end of it a certificate saying "this statement is true to the best of my knowledge and belief." One likes to see someone setting out their stall and saying: "This is what I am going to say so that you may take instructions upon it from your client as to whether or not that is right or not." Simply having a report which contains a number of formal documents, who knows what the witness is going to say about those documents. For example, what he is going to say about a search warrant. Let me give you an example; the witness comes and gives evidence and says: "Well, I conducted a search and I recorded in the search warrant various details but, in fact, what I recorded was incorrect." Simply to serve on us the documents blandly with no other explanation is simply not enough. If he is going to go into detail about the documents he is producing, one wants to know what it is he says about them, because otherwise you cannot plan your cross-examination. Another example; there are witnesses who have no statement of any kind who it is said are going to deal with issues of continuity. I understand the phrase "continuity" to be this. Let us take an example. In a drugs case if you are prosecuting a case in my jurisdiction we would deal with it in this way. You would want to make sure that you could trace the path of the drugs that are recovered from somebody's home from the moment they are seized by a police officer in somebody's house. You want to follow each set of hands who handles that item of drugs right the way through to the time it is placed in the police property store and then when it is taken out of that property store and taken for analysis by the forensic scientist, when it is taken back and put back to the property store. You want to be able to prove by tracing each step that the drugs recovered from the house were the drugs examined by the forensic scientist and those are the drugs that are the subject of the indictment. That is what continuity means. It is a very important element of any case. You have to prove it, because if you do not, you will find at the end of the prosecution's case defence counsel gets up and says: "The prosecution have failed to prove that the item recovered was, in fact, the items examined by the forensic scientist". I am going to use a phrase that my learned fend Mr. Moran has used in this case. It is a belt and braces operation. For the American interpreters amongst you, braces means suspenders. That is what continuity means to me and I suspect to everybody else on this bench. How can we prepare any cross-examination to challenge continuity if no information has been given to us as to what the witness will say? That is the problem in part to which I advert in making this submission to your Honours. What it comes down to is that the prosecution may well say: "We think and therefore cogito ergo sum. We think we have complied, thank you very much, and therefore we have complied." If you look at it carefully, the reality is they have not even begun to comply with the rules which require them, if only in spirit, to give us notice of what is to be said. The point of doing it is to allow this trial to be conducted swiftly and expeditiously. In my submission, if they fail to do this, this Tribunal is going to be faced with a continuing series of applications for adjournments. It is going to save us a lot of time, a lot of heartache if they get on and do what they were required to do. The Tribunal, in my submission, has the opportunity under the rules to introduce a proper procedure, and one of the things that we have discovered on all sides is that we are all learning about how best to implement the procedures of this Tribunal, and the Rule in Rule 89B, I think it is, was plainly contemplating situations which would arise that as we learn how to conduct trials expeditiously, there may need to be things done and rules introduced albeit, as it were, on an informal basis because they are not formally part of the adopted rules, in order to ensure that trials are conducted expeditiously and fairly, and fairly for the defence. What is happening here is that that is not being done by the prosecution, and I have given examples, and I advert to them. It is not being done by the prosecution. There is a remedy which this honourable Tribunal has, which is to say: "Enough is enough. If the prosecution do not do this, they are simply going to be prevented from calling these witnesses", because that is the only just and fair way to deal with it. Set out in the motion signed by all defence counsel a procedure which we would invite this court to adopt, which is one which places very serious restrictions on the prosecution and effectively calls on them to get their act in order. If they do not get their act in order they are simply going to be prevented from springing surprises on us, because that is what it amounts to. If we do not know what these witnesses are going to say, it is prosecution by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may interrupt just for one minute. I am sorry for the rudeness. There is a time limit and we must request a redaction for some disclosure of protected information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am sorry. I am taken by surprise and I do not know what on earth that is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is not a point which he is making. He is saying documents are being supplied every day to the defence. They just come as a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am sorry. I am referring to something else entirely. In the course of his argument defence counsel gave some protected information and because this is open session I do not want to highlight what it is. So the procedure is at some point after it has been done, whoever notices it is supposed to stand up and notify, and I believe the Trial Chamber's law clerk already knows what I am referring to, so that measures can be done to make sure that it does not become part of the public record. All I am asking is that the public record be redacted to take out the one particular piece of protected information that defence counsel has given. I am not speaking to the argument at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Someone had better tell me what I have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please do not take any names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is in connection with a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I do know what I have done and I am terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Names are not really essential for your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am sorry. I did not realise I had done it. I was simply trying to find an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That was observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The Tribunal has my apologies and I do apologise for doing it. Your Honours will realise it is very easy to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. To be on the safe side avoid mentioning names, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It was the difficulty of trying to give an example without leaving everybody completely in the dark as to who I was speaking about. I do apologise. I thank my learned friend for drawing it to my attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, I think that probably comes as a convenient moment for me to say I have had my say and I think I have made the points that I wish to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one quick point as an example involving a witness. One of the witnesses that testified earlier for the Prosecution had both given a written statement to the Prosecution and had given a statement in a court in the former Yugoslavia involving the same set of facts. Months before the trial started those things were served on us. I am working from memory and I may be a little off on dates, but either while this person was actually testifying or the day before, within a very short time of this witness' actual testimony this nice man from the Office of the Prosecutor wandered into our offices and handed us a new copy and a new translation of this document from the former Yugoslavia, complete with a bunch of hand corrections on the document without any explanation of who made these hand corrections, where they came from, whether it was the witness that made them, whether there were some changes in the files in the courts of the former Yugoslavia. Whatever. This just magically appeared in our offices. It is almost like a Chinese water torture. Continually we are getting dribs and drabs, often either immediately before a witness testifies or within a very short period of time before. The day before, two days before a witness is set to testify we are presented with new particular involving a particular witness. At some point this gets to be something that should not occur. At some point we have to say: "Okay. You have got everything." On several occasions it has been things that should have been and appear to have been in the possession of the Prosecutor for some significant period of time. All we are asking, or at least all I am asking, the Trial Chamber to do is say: "Wait a second. Let us give it to the defence counsel a reasonable period of time before this evidence becomes relevant or this witness is going to testify", so we can sit and read it and think about it and try fit it in to where everything else fits in. Just on witness statements, I have got a box with a stack of witness statements, what, about that thick, and frankly being a western lawyer, sometimes the names of the witnesses are a little hard to deal with and where they all fit in, and when suddenly something is dropped in to the middle of this, confusing is I think an understatement, judge. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, may I add a few more arguments in addition to those presented by my learned colleagues, namely the Prosecutor in his response today says that it is not correct that the defence does not know what the witnesses are going to say each when the defence has now been served with the statements of witnesses, referring to the brief note added to the name of the witness. I think in this way they are trying to convey the impression that they have fulfilled their obligation under Rule 67. We wish to underline the obligation of the prosecution under Rule 66A, which clearly states that: "It is the duty of the Prosecutor to supply the defence with all previous statements of Prosecution witnesses". Also Rule 66(B) on reciprocal disclosure immediately, so that the defence may prepare its cross-examination or rather prepare its case. In addition to the names that my colleague Turone mentioned from the list of witnesses, I could add that we still have on the list witnesses under number 53, 56, 69 whose names I may not utter, because I do not know whether they may be protected. So I do not know how the prosecution could have put these people on the list if he has never spoken to those people, and if he does not know what those people could testify about. If the Prosecutor does know, then under Rule 66(B) he is obliged to convey that knowledge to us. It has already been said that this applies in particular to the Politsie witness, General de Vogel, who is under number 46 on the list of witnesses. Not only is the prosecution supplying us with documents with some delay, as my colleagues have noted, in the notice submitted to the court on May 13th, the Prosecutor proposed a list of seven new witnesses who do not appear on the witness list. The Prosecutor surely knows why he is proposing these witnesses and he has probably received some kind of statement from them, or in any other way learned about the facts that these witnesses may testify to, and though these new seven witnesses have been proposed, the defence has not received a single document referring to those witness to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Well, your Honours, may I respond briefly to these further arguments? The main point I would emphasise is that there is absolutely no Rule in our rules which requires necessarily that the prosecution takes the previous statement in any case. Rule 66A simply says that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually I did not understand that sentence. What were you trying to convey?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Rule 66(A) says: "Supporting material which accompanied the indictment when confirmation was sought as well as all prior statements obtained by the Prosecution from the accused or from Prosecution witnesses". That simply means that whenever there is a prior statement the prosecution is compelled to provide defence lawyers with this prior statement, but it might happen for some witnesses that no prior statement exists, as it applies, for instance, with Mr. Beelen and the other examples I gave earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you read Rule 66(A)?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Exactly. Rule 66(A) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: It does say: "As well as all prior statements obtained by the Prosecutor" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: "The Prosecutor shall make available to the defence as soon as practicable after the initial appearance of the accused copies of the supporting ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the relevant thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is exactly what the prosecution did in due time. We provided the defence with all the supporting material and all prior statements obtained by the Prosecutor from the prosecution witnesses. This is exactly what the prosecution did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That was the time practicable after the initial appearance of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. That is what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The ones you are serving only recently?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We provided the defence lawyers with all the supporting material which accompanied the indictment and with all prior statements obtained by the prosecution, by accused and Prosecution witnesses. For a limited number of witnesses as, for instance, Mr. Beelen, the prosecution did not have a real technical witness statement, a prior statement which we could be -- was obtained by the prosecution from this particular witness. The same applies with Mr. Moerbauer, for instance, but what we are now saying in any case we provided the defence lawyers with something which is in any way equivalent to theoretical prior statement so that no surprise there will be when such witnesses will take the stand in this courtroom. Since Mr. Greaves added something concerning Mr. Moerbauer, again I will say the Prosecution is not compelled to have a prior witness statement from Mr. Moerbauer. Mr. Moerbauer is simply a police officer who took part in a police operation concerning the arrest of Mr. Mucic in particular and a number of searches, house searches, which were requested by the Prosecutor of this Tribunal through judicial assistance by the Austrian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. You missed the point really. You picked up that police officer because you know what he is going to depose about. You must -- he must have talked to you. That is a statement to you. Why did you not give the gist -- if you have not recorded a written statement, you can at least inform them: "This is the oral statement he made."

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We have a 50 page report signed by this police officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have you given a copy of that report to the defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Of course we did. We did and we informed our esteemed colleagues on the defence of the existence of this report and the availability for them of this report with a letter written on December 16th 1996. So this report was made available in the original German language and an English translation and in Serbo-Croatian translation a long time ago I would say. We are in May now. So this as far as Mr. Moerbauer is concerned, in this report there is exactly everything concerning the official capacity of this potential witness, about what he exactly did in his official capacity pursuant to an Order of the Austrian investigating judge in judicial assistance with this Tribunal. This was provided to the defence with this report a long time ago. So I would say that they know exactly what Mr. Moerbauer is going to testify on. Of course, they received a copy of the complete material which was seized or anyway the material was put at their disposal many, many months ago, and the possibility of reading this 50 page report signed by Mr. Moerbauer is something absolutely equivalent to a theoretical prior statement which could have been taken by the Prosecution maybe, but it was not, because we decided that when the authorities of a government, a state, provide judicial assistance to this Tribunal carrying on house searches and seizures of documents and provide this Tribunal with the result of this activity, and with a detailed report, this would be absolutely enough, and there is only a requirement, a reason for which a police officer who carried on this activity should be called to the courtroom in order to explain in the courtroom how he proceeded and what happened exactly inside this police operation and so on. As far as the disclosure to the defence lawyers, we did all what we had to do many months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But there is another point made that you still keep on supplying them with statements earlier made by the witnesses. If you had already done that before the trial, then why keep supplying them with further statements? What is the purpose? Then Mr. Moran has made a point that the statements in respect of which earlier he knew during the course of the trial --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Moran has made a point that even though you supplied the statements earlier, now you are supplying them with corrected versions during the course of the trial corrected in their own hands. That is what Mr. Moran is saying. If you have already done that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am sorry. There are some specific details for which I would ask later on my colleague, Mr.s McHenry, to answer, because I joined the team too late, so there are some specific details I am not aware of. So in a moment I will ask Mr.s McHenry to explain some specific details. I want to say that in a general sense the complaint of the defence lawyer that we for a number of witnesses put the defence lawyers in a position not to know absolutely what the witnesses are going to testify on in this court is not true. Another example, for Mr. de Vogel, de Vogel is an expert witness, for which we provided on January 16th, 1997 the CV and a summary, a detailed summary of what he might testify on if he will be actually called into this courtroom. This is another example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is another point also. Ms Residovic has said that you have named certain witnesses, you included them, but have not yet supplied them with what they are going to say. She has given the numbers of those witnesses to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: There is another -- this applies also to what Mr.s McHenry will explain to you quite soon. I think I might give the floor to her. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may not know every specific, but to the extent I can help with a couple of things, the Prosecution has given full and fair disclosure in this case. The defence in this case have all invoked I think it is Rule 66, the provision by which they can even ask for more, and under which they have reciprocal discovery obligations. So we have given them much discovery. We continue to sometimes get new information and when we get it, we give it to them. It does result in material sometimes being given in dribs or drabs, because that is how we have received it. We try, if something is not urgent, to wait until we have several things to give them and then give them to them, but the fact of the matter is as part of full and fair disclosure sometimes things are given in dribs and drabs because sometimes we receive them in dribs or drabs. With respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have not collected all your evidence before the trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour. We have collected most of it. Certainly any evidence we have they have been given but, for instance, we continue to receive documents sometimes from the witnesses, sometimes from another government agency, sometimes from a non-governmental agency. Any time we get something and we intend to use it as evidence, we inform the defence of that. Any time they think they have not received something in sufficient time, something we intend to use as evidence, they have every right when we seek to use it in evidence to object and say: "Your Honour, we just received this yesterday and it is unfair." Then that matter can be litigated, because I mean many of their specifics, as Mr. Turone has indicated are, in fact -- they have been given the material. It is the case to answer a couple of specifics that I am aware of, we do, although I believe we are only required to give Office of the Prosecutor statements -- sometimes there are other statements. Sometimes, for instance, we have received other statements from the Bosnian government. They may not even be reliable. They have may have been given under duress. We may not even know, but if we have such material, we give it to the defence. I believe one example that they mentioned was a statement not taken by the Office of the Prosecutor but by some other non-governmental agency, which we gave to the defence. They had the Office of the Prosecutor statement since I think it was part of the supporting material since the day of the initial arraignment, since we gave all accused, I believe, copies of the supporting material, including witness statements, on the date of the first appearance. It is the case that sometimes there are revised translations. When we get a revised translation, we give it to the defence as soon as we can, but the fact of the matter is when you are dealing with translations sometimes they have to be revised. We are not aware of any prejudice suffered by anyone. We wish that translations were perfect the first time, but that is not the case. So if we give them a revised translation, that is because we are trying to make sure that things are 100 per cent correct, and we give it to them. With respect to another example, for instance with respect, I believe, to some recent witnesses that we have served notice that we may seek to call, we have given an indication of what we will -- that person will testify about. Most of them are about documents and we have previously informed the defence that would be seeking someone to authenticate documents, and that had been done months ago. To the extent that there are Office of the Prosecutor witness statements, they will be given. I know, for instance, in at least one instance there is an Office of the Prosecutor statement, but it is still being transcribed. They will have it well in advance of us seeking leave to use the statement. So I can only say that the prosecution has and will continue to give full and open discovery whenever possible. If we are going to use something as an exhibit, we specifically tell the defence, and if there is some clarification -- for instance, another example is when a witness was here -- I believe Mr. Moran talked about this -- a witness looked at her statement and she made some minor corrections. They are not particularly important, but we believed that it would be fair to give the defence notice that she had made these minor corrections. It had only happened when the witness was here, which was a couple of days beforehand. We gave them to the defence. I was not aware there was any confusion about what they were, but certainly the prosecution is always willing to clarify any confusion to the extent it exists, but I do think when the prosecution is acting fairly and in good faith there is some obligation of the defence to ask us if there is some miscommunication, because, for instance, with Mr. de Vogel, they were given that on January 16th. Now it was not Mr. Greaves. It was prior counsel. Had he asked us about this, we could have shown him the receipt and given him another copy, but there is some obligation for the defence to indicate to us if there is some clarification, because we are trying with respect to all specifics to provide them what we can. I believe if there is any prejudice, they can then object when we seek to bring that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: One quick follow-up on what Miss McHenry just said about that particular witness. This is the first I have heard about who made those corrections, and when they were made. I specifically asked that witness a series of questions: "Did you make these?" "I don't remember". At the same time I asked this witness did the witness talk to anybody about their testimony after they arrived in The Hague. The answer was "No." Under Rule 68, exculpatory evidence, the Prosecutor at that point had the obligation to say: "Judge, time out. What this witness is saying may not be quite right." The prosecution knows exactly which witness I am talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe so. She is not a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Grosdana Cecez.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If it is Mr.s Cecez, that is right. I was not aware there had been any confusion about that. To the extent that Mr.s Cecez did not remember having met me, you certainly brought out she had met me. It was at the end of the a gruelling cross-examination. I believed it was clear -- the facts were clear and that the witness did not do it. So I believe that the defence counsel had all information and had there been any confusion, we would have certainly -- had we known of any confusion, we would have brought it to the attention -- but the fact -- I was not present, for instance, I believe, when she made these corrections. So I still do not believe that, in fact, her testimony was incorrect other than I do believe, as counsel pointed out, she had met me before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this just points out there is something with the system where a witness says: "I don't remember making these corrections. I don't know who made them." I can find it in the transcript if you want me to and I will xerox pages of it. Then she testified at some great length: "No, I had not talked about my testimony here with anybody. The only people I talked to since I have been here were people and we talked about knitting" or that kind of thing. At that point the prosecution I think has an obligation under Rule 68 to stand up and make some corrections. This is absolutely -- this is the very first time I have ever been told who made those corrections on her written statement. If that information was in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor when she denied remembering having done it, I think that is clearly exculpatory for impeachment. It would be in my jurisdiction. I think there was clearly an obligation on the part -- the obligation does not go to Teresa McHenry or any individual Prosecutor. The obligation runs to the Office of the Prosecutor -- I was going to say the sovereign or not -- the entity that is in charge of Prosecution. The entire Prosecution team has that obligation. They should not wait, what, six weeks to make those kinds of disclosures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may be heard about that, because I think it is a very serious allegation, as far as I know the witness stated -- to be frank I do not remember this in detail -- as far as the prosecution is aware, the defence was given and I believe told that these minor corrections had been made by her. If not, I believe that is not a serious issue. All the witness stated was she did not remember. In fact, I do not have an independent recollection of what happened, but certainly if defence counsel is correct, what she stated is she did not remember at that time if she had made them. To the extent that the witness did not remember having met me, defence counsel, I believe, did bring out by her prior statement that she presumably had seen me, whether or not she met me, whether or not she knew who I was. I think that was clear but I do not think that any exculpatory material was fully brought out before the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But do you not indicate when giving a copy of the corrected statement to the defence that she has made these corrections when she has come to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I believe, but, for instance, in that instance I do not know, for instance, that was done in writing, because it is just a matter of you look at it. You decide these are minor corrections. Should we give it to the defence or not? Yes, let's give it to them. Certainly they would have been told and I believe -- I certainly would have thought they would have been told. I can't -- because I was not the person who gave it to the defence counsel -- I can't say that they were or were not told. If Mr. Moran says he wasn't told, I accept that, but in such a case I certainly think then there is some obligation of the defence to ask someone in the Office of the Prosecution: "Well, who exactly did this?" That is what I believe. If the person to whom they are speaking does not know, I certainly think they can bring it to the attention of anyone on this bench and we will all make sure that it is done. I can't -- the prosecution cannot say every single thing works perfectly in every instance. There are many defence counsel. There are many accused and there are many documents. We do everything possible and will continue to do so, but to the extent that sometimes things are not perfect, I do not believe it is fair for the defence to wait until months afterwards and then throw up numerous allegations, many of which can be disproved, many of which would have been clarified, had they raised it, given the amount of disclosure that has gone on here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the explanation that has just been given to you about the witness Grozdana Cecez is a clear example of what we are complaining about. It is extraordinary that no proper note seems to have been kept of when this woman made these alterations, when she said anything at the time when she made these alterations which might be germane to prosecution examining her. That is precisely the point we make. This is just not being done properly. Can I deal with a number of matters that have been raised? The fact of the matter is these documents come to us into our room without any explanation, and I make that absolutely plain. There is not a single note on the document which is sent to us saying: "This is additional evidence" or "this is exculpatory material" and I use those phrases carefully, because exculpatory material has a specific meaning within the rules of this Tribunal. Sometimes it comes at 4.30, 5 o'clock, after we finish court and everybody has dispersed out of the building. It may be that witness has to be cross-examined in the morning and we go away at night not knowing what on earth the purpose of this document is. It is all very well saying: "You can find out when the prosecution get up to examine their own witness." You get taken by surprise and half the evidence gets put before the court before you realise that they are relying on this stuff. It is just not fair. The next matter is this and it is a matter that the learned Judge Jan picked up on. It is if a conversation has been conducted with a witness, that is a statement. Some might think that simply having an oral statement with the witness is a means by which you can get round the Rule 66(A), and that would be an unfortunate thing if it was happening. I make no allegation, but if it was being done for that purpose, it would be unfortunate. Other names come to mind. There is a huge list of people the prosecution now seek to call in addition to their potential witness list. We have no idea what -- sorry. You want to speak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: A huge list of witnesses that the prosecution want to add to their witness first. First of all, we do not know what they are going to say so we do not know whether we need to object to them being put on the witness list. If they are going to say something that is simply informal and innocuous, then one does not object, but if they are going to say something that is important and might put us at some prejudice, how do we know how to formulate an objection to their request to put them on the witness list? Finally I add this. Let us have some more names. Mr. Abribat, Mr. D'Hooge, Lieutenant Gschwendt who I am now told is to be called next week, we have no idea what they are going to say. I know what subjects they are going to talk about but I have no idea of the detail so I can compare versions of those witnesses where they speak about the same matters. In order to be able to properly cross-examine people it is, in my respectful submission, at the very foundation of this Tribunal's Rules that the defence shall be given a reasonable opportunity of knowing what is to be said -- and I have quoted to your Honours in the motion a number of cases from the European Court of Human Rights which set out that very proposition -- a reasonable opportunity of presenting its case to the court under conditions which do not place him at a substantial disadvantage vis-a-vis his opponent. When these things happen a substantial disadvantage is created and it is unjust. The fact we have not complained so far indicates no more than this, that we have been tolerant and have been slowly working out what has been done to us, but we now object to it. We think it is unfair and the pattern of conduct that has been doing on is putting us at, on occasion, substantial disadvantage, not knowing what the purpose of these documents is, not knowing, for example, where they have come from. My learned friend indicates a witness might well have brought their own statement along. It would be interesting to know that because that is a matter we might want to cross-examine the witness about. "Why have you suddenly produced this? Why have you not told anybody about this beforehand when you were being interviewed by the prosecution?" So we are being deprived of small but important bits of information. That is unfair. That is why the defence team, because we have all signed this motion, has put this matter before the court. We have put what I hope is a well ordered procedure by which this court can control this particular problem. It is a simple procedure and one which exists, I suspect, in many of your Honour's jurisdictions, and is there to ensure that Prosecution get their act properly together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So your complaint is about the shortness of notice. That can be sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That is part of it, but I am very concerned about not knowing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As regards the sort of evidence which a new witness is to give, they have to seek our permission before producing a witness not included in the list that at that stage we can always find out what is the purpose and why that particular witness is being examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That will give you enough notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There are often occasions during the course of trial when a point arises that you need to deal with and everybody accepts that that happens in any jurisdiction but it is the rather haphazard way in which it happens which is so disconcerting. If there is a proper framework -- your Honours, of course, are in control of this court and this case -- it gives your Honours an opportunity to control what is happening. To a certain extent we can deal with matters behind the scenes, but your Honours have to be in possession of a regulatory system, if there is a complaint, so that your Honours can deal with it properly. The proposition I have set out before you, which we set out before you is, I hope, a sensible one which gives you a good system by which you can exercise that control. I am perfectly prepared to listen to other suggestions -- alterations as to how you do it, but it is a proposition. It is intended to assist the court to deal with this problem more expeditiously and deal with the problem. I hate going to the Prosecution and complaining. I would rather not have to do that but rather have a well organised system where I do not need to run off to the Prosecution and say "I have not got this. What is this document about and where did this come from?" It would be much nicer if they gave us the information from the word go and then we would not have to do it. It is time-consuming and unfair particularly when it happens late in the afternoon. That is the complaint. Your Honours have been given a system whereby you can control it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we are satisfied with the arguments. We will later give our Ruling on the motion. I think we can proceed to the second one, although we have not received any response on it, the designation of an expert witness. I think you are withdrawing that, or are you still --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe this is Mr. Delic's motion and the prosecution -- we believe that there was a response being filed but maybe it has not made its way, but the short answer is we do not object to Mr. Delic calling the expert witness if he wishes to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is all right. I think we have nothing against that. There is also Prosecution's motions to compel disclosure of addresses of witnesses. I think we have not had a response to that but I know that can be argued.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think there has been a response to that one, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There has been. I filed a response, your Honours, on May 20th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. So I think we can argue that. Can we argue it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is fine with me. Do you want to hear from Prosecution first or would you like to hear from me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is your motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is actually my response. It is their motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are quite right. Any objection to the disclosure of addresses?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You must give material to identify the witnesses, maybe not the addresses. Any objection to the disclosure of their addresses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have to give some material to identify the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The irony, I guess, of the motion filed by the Prosecutor is that some time ago before my arrival the defence had filed a motion asking for the disclosure of the addresses of Prosecution witnesses and the prosecution argued very strenuously against that and gave a lot of reasons why it was inappropriate for us to have the addresses of their witnesses, even though we had said it was very important for us to be able to interview them, talk to them, things of that nature. That is clearly the same reason, the same reason we had, that the prosecution wants us to disclose addresses of our witnesses, so they can go look them up, talk to them, and things of that nature. To so strongly have opposed our request in that regard and then to turn around a month or two later and say: "But we want the address of your witnesses" is just kind of ironic to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is not reciprocal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is not reciprocal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is what has happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You know what the Ruling of the Trial Chamber was to a motion. It said that some identifying material has to be provided. The rule only relates to witnesses for the prosecution but perhaps the same rule can be extended to defence witnesses also. Give some material to the Prosecution by which your defence witness can be identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not think we have any serious objection to giving them some material, but based upon the events that we have been talking about now for the last couple of weeks, and especially considering the physical location of most of these witnesses that we have in mind, and we have not, of course, finished that list yet -- we have still an investigator working -- given in mind their physical location, I would not want to risk putting those witnesses in physical danger. We are in a position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. But if you look at Rule 67(2)(A), I think it is quite specific, especially those cases of alibi and mental deficiency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Rule 67 itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am totally familiar with it. I referred to it in my response. Rule 67 itself is entitled "Reciprocal Disclosure". Reciprocal means when we get something we have to give them its reciprocity. Now they have declined to give us their witness addresses, and therefore there is no reciprocity involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: No, but that is not what 2(A) says. It names what you should do in those cases of alibi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree that is the language of the Rule, your Honour. I have also pointed that out. Let me bring your attention to Rule 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Rule 66(C) I think is poorly drafted because the reasons for Rule 66(C) and for the Prosecutor's ability to protect disclosures under 66(C) apply with equal force to the defence. There is no reason that should be limited to the Prosecutor, because we can find ourselves in the exact position that that Rule contemplates with regard to disclosure. Now my concern, and my concern very clearly, your Honour, is this. Beyond the language of these rules this court has both the power and the obligation to justice in this case, and my concern is this. There was a release of information that was confidential from this court, and we have been talking about it now for the last couple of weeks. We have no idea -- there is no evidence right at this point as to how that information made its way into the public, but it did. It got there somehow. Until it is known what the leak is of information coming out of this building, and we do not know what that leak is, none of us, I do not think, can with confidence publish and distribute around this building information as sensitive as the address of a witness who is living in an area today where he could be subject to immediate retaliation if his name and address became known to some persons in that location. That is what I am resisting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are trying to avoid complying with the provisions of that Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please read 67(A)(2)(B).

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please read it a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You want me to read it out loud, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Any special defence, including that of diminished or lack of mental responsibility, in which case the notification shall specify the names and address was of witnesses and any other evidence upon which the accused intends to rely to establish the special defence".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The names and addresses of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Both in (A) and (B).

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is also unfair because there is no comparable Rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have to take the rules as they are, but we can ask the prosecution not to disclose the information outside --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: They will have to protect whatever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have to take the rule as it is. We cannot say we are going to change the Rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When the names of the witnesses were supplied by the prosecution, they were supplied with requests for protection. They were supplied confidentially. Somehow they made their way outside this chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Violations are natural in human activities. If because one incident has occurred it does not mean that it will keep occurring at every occasion. We will have to abide by the rules. Rules are made to be obeyed. We expect to obey them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem is not with a doctor, a psychiatrist, someone like that, who is going to come and talk about diminished or lack of responsibility. Those either have been or are going to be supplied: names, addresses, CVs, statements. Anything we have on that of course will be supplied to the Prosecution. I am talking about people that are living in an area where tensions have not subsided, who could you threaten by the disclosure of their names and addresses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: And the provision of protection is extended even to the defence. It is not only for Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You are entitled to the same protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it is to be the Ruling of this court that we must comply specifically with (A) (2)(b) by its very terms, then we will be making applications for protection for some of those witnesses just because of the sensitive position they are in where they are living today. We will be doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are entitled to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Beyond that, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will leave it to circumstances, but definitely you are entitled to protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If your witnesses are so endangered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that concludes anything I have to say about the motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will just respond very briefly. Your Honours have pointed out that it is required under the Rules and what the accused is really seeking is an amendment to the Rules. Although it is reciprocal, it is entitled to reciprocal disclosure, there is not exact parody in everything. For instance, in some things the prosecution has to do more. With respect to addresses the rules clearly make a distinction. With all due respect, given that the prosecution has -- the accused by their nature are here because they are accused of serious war crimes, and I think that may explain the drafter's change, but to answer any of Mr. Ackerman's concerns, the prosecution is certainly willing to take extraordinary measures with respect to the disclosure he will give us. We will not provide it to other accused or other defence. I note that previous counsel has supplied us in the beginning with addresses and witness statements of some of his witness, and those have not been disclosed to anyone, and they will not be. So we are certainly prepared, and I believe can work with Mr. Ackerman to make sure that such material is fully protected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we should conclude this debate on this motion. We will give a Ruling later. Should we take number five now, the leave to call Mr. Regis Abribat as a witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just for a minute. Is it the same gentleman recorded --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it the same gentleman who recorded a statement of Mucic in Austria?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: He is, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think Mr. Greaves wanted that investigator called.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I can probably assist as to the point that exists before my learned friend addresses you. In principle he is on -- this man is already on the witness list, so I have assumed that he was going to give evidence or was likely to give evidence. I make that concession and say that I do not object to him being called as a witness, but I make that concession in the light of what I have argued this morning on the motion earlier on. So I think that may shortcircuit what my learned friend has to say. In principle I do not object to him being called, but it is subject to the Ruling that you are going to have to give in the other matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: And, your Honour, to this motion on leave to call Mr. Regis Abribat, I would like to put even another name orally pertaining to the same matter, because this is, as your Honours will recall -- comes out of what Mr. Greaves said on Thursday, 8th May for the first time during the proceedings, and made serious allegations of oppression in connection with what happened with Mr. Mucic when he was interviewed in Vienna. To this there has surfaced a new person, an Austrian police officer by the name of Hansel Gschwendt, who was present when Mucic appeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Give up his right to counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes. I have already informed Mr. Greaves we have would like to put this name of Hansel Gschwendt on our list. As I understand it, we already have his support to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I make the same comment about Gschwendt. I do not object to him being called but it is subject to my observation, I have already made.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Quite obviously he is talking about the circumstances -- your grievance was that earlier he had been insisting that he must have counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Then suddenly he changes his mind and says he does not want counsel. So you have a good opportunity to examine the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I hope my concession that I have made is a helpful one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes the argument from my side, your Honours. I ask for leave for these two persons to be put on the witness list, the names being Mr. Regis Abribat and Mr. Hansel Gschwendt. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg I think you are concerned with the next motion, the motion to specify the documents disclosed that the Delalic defence intend to use and serve. Is that your motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I give the floor to Ms McHenry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I want to know how long it will take because I do not think it is anything on the short side. No response has been received by the defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have you filed any response to the last motion? It is not before me. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): We are prepared to respond during the hearing, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You could respond. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): We can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. In terms of the prosecution presentation, it will be very brief. I mean, we have made our motion and I think the issue is -- I have discussed this at length with Ms Residovic outside the courtroom. I think there is a clear issue in dispute but I do not think it is a particularly time-consuming one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This being the last thing on the list, we either take this motion and close for the day, against coming back tomorrow morning or we adjourn and come in the afternoon but I prefer my first suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: May I be heard on that also? That goes to our witness list, your Honour, and our possibilities of tomorrow bringing witnesses. I could bring my witness list immediately if it could be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Today?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: This is how it goes. Our next witness will be Dr O.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can bring him tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: He can be here tomorrow at 2.30 at the earliest. Our second witness will be, depending on the leave of the Trial Chamber, Mr. Regis Abribat, and our third witness would be Mr. Bart D'Hooge and the fourth is Mr. Hansel Gschwendt. On the orders. I say nothing specific about the orders. These are the four we can envisage to start with certainty on Monday morning. Dr O seems to arrive at a time that he can be heard tomorrow at 2.30. It is up to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
