utterances.text: It is all right. We can cope with that. We will take this motion now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: And see if we can finish in time and close for the day until tomorrow morning. So let us hear Mr.s McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the -- I will not repeat what is in my motion. The motion sets out more explicitly what the details are, but the general issues is what is meant under both the prosecution and under the reciprocal obligations of the prosecution and defence with the requirement that the other party must be allowed to inspect the material that may be used in evidence. As I have indicated in this case, the defence have sought the discovery, including things that may be material to the preparation of their defence and they have now reciprocal discovery obligations under which they and the prosecution are required to allow the other party to inspect the material that will be used as evidence during the trial. In this case the prosecution has given the defence access to large material. In fact, this would almost be considered an open file kind of discovery. We could have certainly said to the defence: "We are giving you all these thousands of documents and we may use all of them in evidence." We did not think that was fair or consistent with the spirit or the letter of the law. So we provide all the material and then to the extent we intend to use something as evidence, we specifically notify the defence: "This will be used as evidence in trial". In response we have asked the defence to indicate to us which material they will use as evidence in trial, as they are required to do, and they have indicated certain documents they have given us and said: "We intend to use these", but with respect to hundreds, and I would guess even more than that, thousands of documents that the Prosecution had provided to the defence, either because they were seized from the accused or because we received them from the Bosnian government, the defence states: "We reserve the right to use any of these." Because some of these documents have not been translated into English, for instance, and they are not required to be -- they are originally in Serbo-Croatian -- or, to be frank, with respect to some of the documents from the Bosnian government we do not believe are reliable, we are in a position of not knowing in effect what the defence is going to use in evidence. Therefore, we do not know which documents to get translated. We do not know which documents we need to investigate to seize if, in fact, they are authentic. So we believe that just as the prosecution is required to specifically and in good faith give a specific listing of what items will be used rather than an all-encompassing everything, the defence should be required to do the same. Now, we have indicated, of course, that we do not expect anything they tell us now or in the near future to be 100 per cent final. Of course things are going to change. It may depend on exactly what the prosecution does. It may depend on additional material they find. It may depend on their own investigation. The prosecution is not asking for 100 per cent final list such that they will never be allowed to use anything else, but we are asking for a good faith reporting of exactly what at the present time they intend to use in evidence. That is the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Supposing the defence states that they intend to use all the documents. They can, of course, give certain documents when they enter upon defence. What are you going to do then?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: As the prosecution has stated many times --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All these documents have been supplied by you to the defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: All the documents have been provided to the defence as part of disclosure. The prosecution has not said they find them reliable or even have them translated, know exactly what each of them means. That's right. It is, as the prosecution has stated many times before -- we have the utmost respect, both professional and personal, for Ms Residovic, and I, in fact, do not believe that Ms Residovic could or would in good faith stand up and say: "We are going to introduce to the Trial Chamber the thousands of documents." In fact, we attached a letter that Mr. Ostberg had written to Ms Residovic that said: "Please advise us whether, in fact, it is your intention to use every single document". The response there. I do not believe the response indicates they intend to use every single document. I believe, and also from the conversations with Mr.s Residovic, what she reserves is her right to use any of the documents, but she does not, and I would submit frankly cannot in good faith say that she intends to use every single one of these thousands of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we hear Ms Residovic on the motion? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I can state here that as the defence counsel of Mr. Delalic and the whole defence team will fully abide by the obligations envisaged by the statute and the rules of this Tribunal. Only by respect of those rules and their strict implementation puts me in a position to act in good faith and only by acting in that way can I defend my client. Allow me to say that I am extremely surprised by the request of the prosecution, which is not grounded in the obligations of the defence according to the rules. Before giving an explanation, the defence would propose that this request of the prosecution be rejected. I will explain myself further. It is 29th May 1997 today. I may call it famous or infamous year has gone by since 29th May 1996, when the defence of Mr. Delalic proposed the implementation of the provision, of article 66(B) -- of Rule 66(B), and whenever it had at its disposal any document, it disclosed it to the Prosecution so that the prosecution has received from Mr. Zejnil Delalic's defence a large number of documents, some of which it will use as evidence in these proceedings. Since then the defence of Zejnil Delalic has submitted to the Prosecution, although it is not obliged to do so by the rules, but in the interests of the defence, in the interests of the efficiency of the proceedings, in the interest of the prosecution gaining access to exculpatory material, we served on the prosecution 30 statements of witnesses. On that basis the prosecution conduct hearings, interrogations of a large number of people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and some of those appear on their list of witnesses. This conduct on the part of the defence counsel of Mr. Zejnil Delalic is not only an open file approach and full compliance with the Rule 66(B) and 67(C), so that I cannot understand this objection on the part of the prosecution that possibly it has failed in some respect in fulfilling its obligations. Allow me to add that in addition to this kind of conduct throughout 1996 we have received, I must admit, a large number of documents from the prosecution, but since we had to have a ruling by the Trial Chamber to receive the statement of Mr. Mucic, which the prosecution had in its possession since May, but we received it much later. Also other documents reached us mostly in December 1996, but they were dated, some of them, in 1995. What I said already before regarding the way in which we received those documents, even if we did receive them we did not receive them as efficiently as we should have and as the defence has sought to do in fully respecting rules 66(B) and 67(C). Allow me now to refer to the crux of the problem we have before us. When we ask for addresses and other data on Prosecution witnesses, we know what the answer was. I have already said that in the interest of a fair trial, and I wish to contribute to it, we provided statements together with all the addresses of witnesses. What is the prosecution asking of us now? It is asking for something that I do not consider to be an obligation stipulated in any rule of our Rules of Procedure, namely the prosecution again after the Ruling of this Trial Chamber that all material be disclosed to us and served on us, which was seized during the search of the premises, private and business offices of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, the Trial Chamber ruled that all the material be returned to us that will not be used in preparation of the trial. The date of that ruling is October 9th, 1996. The prosecution returned to us among the written papers only one document, an ID card. As for videotapes, we received 30. 4,000 papers of various kinds which have nothing to do with this trial have been kept by the prosecution, and we were supplied with photocopies of those materials, and they did so -- they also provided about 60 video tapes following the ruling of the Trial Chamber. Our obligation, according to 67(c) is, referring to the provisions of 66(B): "The prosecution is entitled to examine all books, documents, photographs and tangible objects in his custody or control". Your Honours, those are documents and objects which the prosecution has been holding since 18th March 1996 in the original, which it is analysing, translating and doing whatever it considers necessary, and copies of which have been served on the defence. I do not know what the prosecution expects of us. Copies of the documents that they have been holding for more than a year. So I really do not understand this request on the part of the prosecution for some kind of an obligation regarding materials that are already in their possession. We have tried to explain to the Prosecution that they should act in accordance with the decision of 9th October. Return to us all the originals, and then if we feel that we need to show you again something that you have already seen, then we will do it, but as you have not done that, we do not know what we can disclose to you when you are holding everything. That is one side of this issue. Regarding other documents, they were received from our government. When those documents were supplied, we received copies of those documents. Again we do not know, nor do we see anywhere in the rules where is our obligation for them to examine any document which we now have because they were given to you by the prosecution, for them to look at again, though they can look at them every day because they have them in their offices. That is why we feel that our obligation has been fully complied with. Under 67(c) it says cumulatively that Prosecution should be given all books, documents, photographs, tangible objects, and the prosecution is already in possession of those and also what evidence we intend to use. The defence has no obligation to provide a list of witnesses or list of documents that it intends to use in the trial. We have a Ruling to that effect from this Trial Chamber. But who can tell the defence which of the documents among the 4,000 it will use? It depends on the presentation of the case by the prosecution. We maybe use 4, 400 or 40. We may even end the defence of my client with the presentation of evidence on the part of the prosecution. Therefore, again we do not see any reason for this request nor do I see any obligation that the defence might have to fulfil any obligation has been explained in this motion on the part of the prosecution. I repeat once again that the defence gave to the Prosecution in January in addition to everything it gave in 1996 also precise indications of documents, more than 100. I do not think that the prosecution could have collected as many in two years of its investigation which it will be using in the proceedings. So we feel that the defence has absolutely no obligation on the basis of the statute or the Rules of Procedure with respect to the Prosecution, that it has fulfilled all its obligation in time and immediately and in the future if it gains possession of any document or object which the prosecution does not have, it will supply them with it. I do not know whether there is any need for any further explanations. I think that we are now in a situation in which we again are confronted with the question whether the prosecution is serving on us all the material it has. Unfortunately I cannot provide the name of the witness, but according to my investigation in the field, I learned that the prosecution is taking some statements from witnesses, and I would like to ask the prosecution whether it is indeed doing that or is it correct for the defence to find that out, as we did in the case of Mr. Hadzihuseinovic. So I think we come back to the previous question. The defence of Delalic has fully complied with its obligation and we will seek to do that in the future as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you any replies to what has been said, essentially the last statements about continuing taking of statements?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the case that the prosecution, yes, is continuing to take statements, and if they are relevant to the material of the preparation of the defence, or the prosecution intends to seek leave to call the person as a witness, the defence will get a copy of the statement. The only other thing that I would add is, Ms Residovic is correct that she has given us, and I tried to say this in my initial argument -- notice of some documents she will use and we are satisfied with that disclosure. The only issue has to do with the obligation and in this case it is the same obligation for both the prosecution and the defence, to allow the other side to inspect material that may be used in trial. The prosecution did not and would not think it fair under the letter and spirit of these rules, which we believe must be read reasonably, to give them 4,000 documents and say we may use these in trial. It is exactly the same for the defence and we believe it is up for your Honours to interpret the rule. It will apply to both sides equally. We believe that the rules must be read reasonably and must be a reasonable attempt to specify what, in fact, will be used in trial. That is everything. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we will give a Ruling on this matter later, because it is not as difficult as it is envisaged. Now because of the difficulties we have had for the past two weeks I think we should tomorrow morning try and have a status conference to reassess how you are readjusting to the bringing of your witnesses. We have tried for some time to find out how long it might take you to conduct the case of the prosecution, so that we will have an estimate of how much the defence also will organise itself. So tomorrow morning at 10.00 am we would like to have a status conference. Then at 2.30 we can now carry on with your witnesses. That should complete the proceedings of the week. The Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble tomorrow morning. (12.50pm)
